https://theconversation.com/horrors-mons.title: Horror’s monsters find new meaning with queer and trans audiences – how ‘Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma’ dissects identity
https://theconversation.com/horrors-mons.summary: Horror as a genre has traditionally been rife with transphobia and homophobia. But LGBTQ+ fans love it anyway.
https://theconversation.com/horrors-mons.text: Queer horror is having a moment. The recent film “ Leviticus ” (2026), a harrowing allegory for conversion therapy , was a critical hit. Meanwhile, Ryan Murphy’s undeniably gay “ American Horror Story ” returned to TV this fall, offering a campier approach to the genre. But queer people’s fascination with horror is by no means new. For trans and queer viewers, horror has long acted as a mirror to reflect on complex personal questions of identity and embodiment. Another new film, Jane Schoenbrun’s “ Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma ” (2026), explores queer people’s relationship with horror. Schoenbrun’s film isn’t really a horror movie; it’s a movie about horror movies . The protagonist, a young auteur named Kris, is rebooting an old slasher franchise, “Camp Miasma.” The franchise has aged poorly, and she wants to update the film for a contemporary audience. “This part’s transphobic!” Kris mutters while watching the original film. But Kris is also helplessly obsessed with “Camp Miasma,” and Schoenbrun’s film suggests that it’s precisely the slasher’s troubling, problematic elements that have enthralled her. As both a trans studies scholar and a longtime horror fan, I know how she feels. In fact, Kris’ complicated relationship with “Camp Miasma” may feel deeply familiar for many queer and trans viewers. Horror has produced some of the most objectionable queer- and trans-coded characters in cinema history. These portrayals of LGBTQ+ people as monstrous and pathological can be found in films ranging from the low-budget slashers that inspired Schoenbrun – most notably “ Sleepaway Camp ” (1983) – to Oscar winners such as “ The Silence of the Lambs ” (1991). Yet queer and trans audiences have often found themselves strangely drawn to these films and to the horror genre overall . Why does a genre that has treated LGBTQ+ people so poorly keep them coming back? No one’s 20s and 30s look the same. You might be saving for a mortgage or just struggling to pay rent. You could be swiping dating apps, or trying to understand childcare. No matter your current challenges, our Quarter Life series has articles to share in the group chat, or just to remind you that you’re not alone. ‘Heartstopper’ is helping LGBTQ+ fans find hope and community across time and space Childhood experiences of LGBTQ+ stigma can harm romantic relationships decades later – psychologists explain how to reconnect with yourself and your partner Heated Rivalry shows how queer joy can disrupt hockey’s culture of masculinity Queerness is baked into the very structure of the horror genre. Film scholar Robin Wood summarized the horror formula as “Normality is threatened by the Monster.” As Wood points out, the social order that represents “normality” is often tied to heteronormative structures like the nuclear family and the heterosexual couple. Horror stages gleeful attacks on this order: Think of the family under siege by malevolent spirits, or the straight camp counselors hacked to bits after having sex. Such themes may resonate strongly for queers who find their goals and desires in tension with a society primarily built around cisgender, heterosexual life paths. Beyond its social elements, horror also offers queer and trans people a personal encounter with an aspect of themselves that they may find confusing or even upsetting: their bodies. Feminist scholar Carol Clover argued that horror is a “ body genre ,” meaning it is intended to activate a bodily response in the viewer. Often, one of the ways horror elicits this physical response is through the visceral, violent onscreen deformation of bodies. In body horror , the human body is depicted as an unruly, often disgusting and always vulnerable accumulation of flesh , blood and guts. Such images can mirror and affirm the difficult feelings that many queer and trans folks have experienced with regard to embodiment, their distress surrounding the forms their bodies take or the desires they feel. Horror’s depiction of monsters and monstrous bodies have allowed many queer and trans people to take ownership over their experiences of personal pain and social stigma. As trans theorist Susan Stryker put it, “I want to lay claim to the dark power of my monstrous identity without using it as a weapon against others or being wounded by it myself.” Other queer and trans writers, however, have asked about the limits of identifying with monstrosity. “How does building an identity on reclaiming the boogeyman affect the psyche ?” wonders critic Grace Byron. Horror, after all, centers on violence, brutality, fear and even death. Identifying with these forces might feel powerful in the moment, but it doesn’t necessarily help reckon with the real violence that led LGBTQ+ people to identify with them in the first place. When I teach horror , my students and I talk about how we might approach some of the most transphobic figures in the horror canon. Instead of identifying with these “monsters,” we try to think critically about the conditions that created them. Take the trans-coded serial killer Buffalo Bill, from “The Silence of the Lambs.” Scholar Cael Keegan argues that “The Silence of the Lambs” raises issues of state violence against transgender people. Similarly, scholar Grace Lavery reads Buffalo Bill as a victim of medical gatekeeping , which bars lifesaving gender-related care from those who need it. Rather than either rejecting characters like Buffalo Bill or embracing their monstrosity, queer viewers and their allies could instead ask what these characters show about the structural conditions that keep queer and trans people at the margins of society. When my students approach horror, I encourage them to consider the strategy that queer theorist José Esteban Muñoz offers for minority groups engaging with harmful representations in dominant culture: disidentification . For Muñoz, to “disidentify” means refusing to see yourself in images that degrade you, yet still finding ways of making those violent representations generative for your own thinking, dreaming and living. “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma” is about disidentifying with horror. It acknowledges the harmful, long-standing transphobia of the genre. And it is also frank about the disturbing prevalence of sexual violence in horror, both onscreen and behind the scenes . But the queer characters in “Camp Miasma” – both in Schoenbrun’s film and in its fictional counterpart – still manage to connect with themselves and their bodies. And I think they do this not just by watching horror, but by watching themselves watch horror. So perhaps the draw of horror for queer and trans people isn’t just that it lets them identify with onscreen monsters or victims of violence. It’s that it gives them the opportunity to reflect on these identifications – and to reject them or transform them. In the process of finding meaning in horror’s monstrous worlds, queer and trans people tap into their own power to respond to the monstrous world around them.

https://theconversation.com/for-centurie.title: For centuries, bird migration was a mystery – a tech revolution is changing that, and could help save these amazing creatures
https://theconversation.com/for-centurie.summary: An early clue came from storks found in Europe with African arrows in their bodies. Today, an atlas reveals hundreds of bird migration routes that are both complicated and remarkable.
https://theconversation.com/for-centurie.text: For more than 2,000 years , scientists have scratched their heads over one of the most basic mysteries of the natural world: Where do birds go? Billions of birds appear and disappear with the seasons every year. Early naturalists offered explanations for the disappearances that today seem fantastical: Birds transformed into other species , one theory went. Others suggested they hibernated underwater or even migrated to the moon . The truth, that these small animals were traveling thousands of miles across the planet, must once have seemed just as improbable. Then, in the early 1800s, dramatic evidence emerged supporting the theory of migration. White storks began appearing in Germany with African arrows embedded in their bodies. These birds became known as pfeilstörche , or “arrow storks .” They provided compelling evidence that birds disappearing from Europe were traveling all the way to Africa and back. Almost two centuries later, scientists are still asking the same question, but our ability to answer it has been transformed. For most of ornithological history, scientists understood migration through brief glimpses of a bird, a specimen collected somewhere else, or the rare instance of a banded bird recovered hundreds or thousands of miles from where it had been marked. From these fragments of intelligence, scientists reconstructed journeys that took place largely beyond their view. Today, it’s possible to see the journeys themselves, almost in real time. Bird banding was the first tool used to attempt a systematic approach to connect these fragments of information. Since the early 1900s, researchers have placed uniquely numbered metal bands on birds and hoped someone, somewhere, would encounter them again. Of more than 79 million birds banded, only about 6.5 million have been recovered . That generally told scientists just two things: where a bird was banded and where it was encountered again. Everything between them remained invisible. Over the past quarter-century or so, the tools used to determine where birds go have changed dramatically. Tracking devices can now be carried by increasingly smaller birds, recording their movements and communicating with land-based receivers or satellites orbiting the earth. Testing stable isotopes in feathers and other tissues can reveal where a bird originated. Genetic testing can distinguish populations. At the same time, the extraordinary growth of bird-watching and citizen science has created another revolution. Millions of observations by bird-watchers submitted to eBird , an online database to record the birds they see, show the distribution and abundance of birds across a continent throughout the year in ways early ornithologists could scarcely have imagined. Collectively, these methods open an extraordinary new window into migratory birds and one of nature’s most remarkable behaviors: migration. More than 70% of North American bird species are migratory. Yet scientists have known surprisingly little about where specific populations go. A species like the American robin may breed across thousands of miles of North America, with different breeding populations migrating to entirely different places for the winter. Birds breeding in one part of the continent may travel one route and encounter one set of environmental conditions, while members of the same species experience a completely different set of conditions along another route. These connections between where a bird breeds and where it spends the winter is called migratory connectivity . They are critical for understanding everything from the consequences of climate change on birds to how avian pathogens and diseases spread, to a species’ basic ecology. We are ornithologists and conservation scientists who have spent almost 15 years along with a team of contributors compiling this rapidly expanding knowledge on bird movement into The Atlas of North America’s Migratory Birds . It is being published Nov. 3, 2026, by Princeton University Press, with all profits going to bird conservation and research in Latin America and the Caribbean. The atlas covers the latest information on seasonal movements for nearly 600 species and combines a century of bird-banding data with eBird observations, tracking studies, stable isotope testing, genetics and other sources of information. What emerges is a picture of migratory birds that is both more complicated and more remarkable than the simple arrows pointing between breeding and wintering ranges on a map. Consider the yellow-billed cuckoo . These birds breed over a wide range of the eastern two-thirds of the U.S. but migrate to a relatively small wintering area in the Gran Chaco region of northern Argentina, Paraguay and southern Bolivia. In contrast, peregrine falcons that breed in Alaska migrate almost directly south, dispersing across the Americas to wintering grounds that extend as far as southern South America. Discoveries like these are accumulating rapidly. Collectively, they amount to a renaissance in our understanding of animal movement never before imagined. The more clearly scientists can follow individual birds and populations across the planet, the more extraordinary these species can seem. Migratory birds such as the arctic tern and northern wheatear cross oceans, deserts and mountain ranges. Some, like the bar-tailed godwits, fly thousands of miles without stopping . Others, like the American redstart, return year after year to remarkably precise breeding and wintering locations. They navigate landscapes and respond to winds, weather, food and environmental conditions across enormous geographic scales. We see these species and their migrations as among evolution’s great living masterpieces. That’s why we combined science with natural history and artist John Anderton’s extraordinary illustrations of the birds themselves. The maps allow us to see where birds travel, and the art brings the species to life. Together, they make visible something that humans could only imagine for most of our history. North America has lost about 3 billion birds during the past half-century, and many migratory species continue to decline. To understand why a population is declining and help save it, researchers need to understand the species’ entire annual cycle: its critical stopover habitats, wintering grounds and threats along its migration routes. For much of the history of ornithology, scientists studied birds primarily during their breeding season. That made practical sense. Birds are conspicuous then – singing, defending territories, building nests and raising young. But a migratory bird may spend only a few months of its life in its breeding grounds. Conditions such as weather, food availability and habitat quality encountered during migration can determine whether an individual survives to breed again . Drought thousands of miles away can affect a bird’s condition months later. American redstarts depart later after dry winters and produce fewer young . Declining horseshoe crab populations in Delaware Bay have reduced food availability for migrating red knots , contributing to lower survival . All of this knowledge has accumulated because people value birds and have devoted enormous time and effort to understanding them. For more than a century, thousands of bird-banders have woken up before the crack of dawn to set traps, carefully place bands on birds’ legs and release them, often knowing the chances of ever learning what happened to those individuals were exceedingly small. More recently, tracking technology has allowed researchers to follow individual birds across continents and oceans . Those tracks exist because scientists, students, technicians and others have spent countless hours attaching and recovering tags, and contributing and sharing their data. https://phys.org/news/2026-10-amino-acid.summary: New research started with a special material that behaves unusually when it's extremely cold—135 degrees below zero Fahrenheit (minus 93 degrees Celsius), close to the most frigid temperature ever recorded in Antarctica—and showed that the unusual behavior could be extended to well above room temperature—up to about 135 F (57 degrees Celsius), close to the highest heat ever measured in Death Valley, California.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-ai-chatbot.title: Most AI chatbots stay in the political middle ground, with Grok being an exception
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-ai-chatbot.summary: The 2026 election was the first parliamentary election in Sweden since AI chatbots became a serious part of everyday life—not least for young people and first-time voters. Today, it is possible to turn to a number of services, such as ChatGPT, to get information about politics, reason about political issues or get help polishing arguments. Discussions have also arisen in society about whether political values are expressed in AI-generated texts and, if so, which ones.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-dna-underw.title: DNA and underwater footage reveal two new species of deep-sea siphonophores
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-dna-underw.summary: New research is shedding light on the diversity of deep-sea siphonophores. A team of scientists from MBARI, the University of Gdańsk, New York University and Yale University conducted a comprehensive examination of Bargmannia siphonophores using museum material, submersible observations and genomic sequencing. This work uncovered two previously unknown species: Bargmannia marlena and Bargmannia pyrosa. The team published their findings in the Zoological Journal of the Linnean Society last week.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-canine-can.title: Canine cancer patients contribute to next-generation minimally invasive cancer therapies for dogs and humans
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-canine-can.summary: Natural disasters. Hikes. Long, dark nights alone. For many people, dogs offer a sense of safety and comfort in challenging or uncertain times. Cancer researchers at a new lab at Purdue University are partnering with dogs to make cancer less frightening—and less deadly—to some of humanity's very best friends using a technique called tumor ablation.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-natural-fo.title: Natural forest regeneration helps curb spread of invasive species
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-natural-fo.summary: The presence of non-native trees is often seen as an obstacle to the recovery of tropical forests regrowing in previously deforested areas. To better understand the behavior of these plants over time in both humid and dry forests, researchers from approximately 60 institutions analyzed data from over 1,500 areas of forest regeneration across the Americas. The results, published in the journal Nature Plants, indicate that the initial dominance of exotic species is temporary. They multiply easily during the first 10 to 20 years, taking advantage of abundant sunlight in open areas. However, they decline as native trees grow and shade the forest.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-assumption.title: The assumption about farm automation that may be wrong
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-assumption.summary: You've likely heard this assumption: When AI-enabled and autonomous machines arrive on the farm, jobs will disappear. But researchers at the University of California, Davis, who studied 16 fruit tree operations in California and Washington for three years, found that automation still takes human knowledge. What changes is how the work gets done. The study, drawing on 165 in-depth interviews with workers and growers, was published in the journal New Technology, Work and Employment.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-health-rew.title: Public health programs can 'rewire' social networks, study finds
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-health-rew.summary: An educational program intended to improve maternal and child health fundamentally altered the social fabric of the rural Honduran villages where it was implemented, a new Yale-led study finds. The findings, researchers say, have implications for interventions anywhere that seek to improve people's well-being by disseminating information or changing behaviors through social contagion.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-disiplinan.title: Disiplinang walang palo: Challenging common Filipino parenting misbeliefs
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-disiplinan.summary: More frequent spanking is linked to greater anxiety and aggression in children over time, according to international research that includes Filipino families presented by psychology professor Dr. Liane Peña Alampay of the Ateneo de Manila University. The findings challenge the familiar belief that "pamamalo" produces more disciplined children, pointing instead to the benefits of warm relationships in the home, clear expectations and nonviolent disciplining.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-stream-bio.title: Stream restoration improves biodiversity but not necessarily ecosystem functioning
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-stream-bio.summary: The EU Nature Restoration Regulation adopted in 2024 establishes the restoration of ecosystem functions as an objective of stream restoration. But can conventional measures that focus primarily on restoring the physical structure of rivers and streams fulfill this task?

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-pandemic-p.title: Study: Pandemic arrest patterns may have deepened existing inequalities in policing
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-pandemic-p.summary: The COVID-19 pandemic was a public health crisis that affected more than the public's health. It brought complex changes across many aspects of society, including having an influence on suburban arrest patterns, according to a study co-authored by University at Buffalo researchers.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-ants-basic.title: Ants break a basic rule of biology to help them adapt to new environments
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-ants-basic.summary: A new study led by researchers in the Eco-Evo-Devo lab at the University of Ottawa finds that ants can decouple antenna size from both head and body size as they develop into different social castes, revealing how social signals and hormones help shape traits for specialized colony roles.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-microplast.title: Microplastics in sediment could trace decades of human activity worldwide
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-microplast.summary: In a review article recently published in the journal Earth-Science Reviews, researchers from the Leibniz Institute for Baltic Sea Research Warnemünde (IOW), in collaboration with colleagues from the University of Leicester (United Kingdom), report on how human activity has altered Earth's sediments over the decades.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-d.title: Discrimination fuels mental health crisis among LGBTQ+ youth, national report finds
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-d.summary: LGBTQ+ youth continue to face high rates of anxiety, depression and suicidal thoughts, driven by ongoing discrimination, a new report says.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-l.title: Researchers show how leukemia cells 'hide' from treatment
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-l.summary: In a first-of-its-kind study collaboration, new research has uncovered that chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) cells may switch between different survival signals, helping explain why treatments work well for some patients but stop working for others. These findings could ultimately help pave the way for more personalized treatment.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.title: Clinical support tool helps primary care health professionals detect and treat chronic kidney disease
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.summary: Investigators have developed and validated a clinical decision support tool to improve the diagnosis and treatment of chronic kidney disease (CKD) at the point of care. The research was presented at ASN Kidney Week 2026, Oct. 22–25.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-p.title: Potassium binder may ease the burden of dietary potassium restriction in people on dialysis
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-p.summary: Dietary potassium restriction is important for managing hyperkalemia, or high blood potassium levels, in individuals on maintenance hemodialysis, but it imposes a substantial day-to-day burden. Results from a recent clinical trial indicate that adding the potassium binder sodium zirconium cyclosilicate (SZC) may help. The findings will be presented at ASN Kidney Week 2026, Oct. 22–25.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-f.title: Fruits and vegetables outperform medication for treating metabolic acidosis in chronic kidney disease
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-f.summary: In people with chronic kidney disease (CKD), oral sodium bicarbonate is a standard treatment for metabolic acidosis (too much acid buildup in the body), but results from a recent clinical trial indicate that dietary acid reduction with base-producing fruits and vegetables may be a better option. The findings will be presented at ASN Kidney Week 2026, Oct. 22–25.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-s.title: Social determinants linked with kidney failure risk among survivors of critical illness and acute kidney injury
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-s.summary: New research indicates that certain individual- and neighborhood-level social determinants of health may increase the risk of developing postdischarge kidney failure in patients who developed acute kidney injury while in intensive care. The findings will be presented at ASN Kidney Week 2026 Oct. 22–25.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-s.title: Standardized kidney biopsy protocol is safe in high-risk patients
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-s.summary: Results from a prospective study reveal that with standardized precautions, even high-risk patients may safely undergo a kidney biopsy, a cornerstone of kidney diagnostics that is often perceived as dangerous in certain vulnerable patient populations. The findings were presented at ASN Kidney Week 2026, Oct. 22–25.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.title: US cannabis legalization linked to rise in cardiovascular hospital admissions
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.summary: Legalization of recreational cannabis in the U.S. is associated with a rise in hospital admissions for cardiovascular disease, finds an analysis of more than 50 million patient discharge records, published in the open-access journal BMJ Open.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-e.title: Early uptake for oral semaglutide proves rapid relative to injectables
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-e.summary: Early uptake was rapid for oral semaglutide (Wegovy pill) relative to injectable incretin-based weight management therapies, according to a study published online Oct. 13 in Annals of Internal Medicine.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.title: Beyond the ACE score: A single number may miss the complexity of childhood trauma, study suggests
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.summary: For years, childhood trauma has often been measured with a simple score. The widely used adverse childhood experiences, or ACEs, system assigns points for experiences such as abuse, neglect, parental divorce, substance abuse in the home and other adversities before age 18. In general, the higher the score, the greater the risk for future health and behavioral problems.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.title: ADHD medication unlikely to raise risk of self-harm, international study finds
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.summary: The risk of self-harm among people with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is highest before people start ADHD medication, rather than after treatment begins, according to new research led by Aston University and recently published in the journal BMJ Mental Health.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.title: Adults with type 1 diabetes more likely to have depressive, anxiety symptoms
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.summary: Adults with type 1 diabetes have a higher prevalence of depressive and generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) symptoms than those with type 2 diabetes or without diabetes, according to a research letter published online Oct. 20 in the Annals of Internal Medicine.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-n.title: Nurses are an important resource in Swedish bowel cancer screening
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-n.summary: Colonoscopies performed by specially trained nurses as part of the Swedish bowel cancer screening program are of at least the same quality as those performed by doctors, according to a study from Karolinska Institutet published in the journal Endoscopy. The results suggest that nurses could help to address the increasing demand for examinations within the national screening program.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-i.title: Imaging study links several schizophrenia symptoms to a single brain signal
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-i.summary: Schizophrenia is often described as a list of separate problems. People may perceive the world differently, act on their surroundings differently or speak in ways that are hard to follow. A new study has found that a single brain signal may help explain a range of seemingly unrelated schizophrenia symptoms.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-i.title: Intermittent fasting plus exercise boosts fat loss and fitness in 12-week obesity trial
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-i.summary: A research team led by the Joint University Institute for Sport and Health (iMUDS) at the University of Granada, in collaboration with the Granada Institute for Biomedical Research and the Biomedical Research Network Center, has studied the effects of combining intermittent fasting and supervised exercise in people with obesity as part of the TEMPUS project.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-p.title: Prevalence of binge eating 40.5% in U.S. high school students
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-p.summary: The prevalence of binge eating at least one day in the past 30 days is 40.5% in U.S. high school students, according to a study published online Oct. 15 in Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.title: Common multiple sclerosis treatment linked to bowel disease risk
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.summary: People with multiple sclerosis (MS) who are treated with rituximab have an increased risk of developing inflammatory bowel disease, particularly Crohn's disease, although the absolute risk remains low. This is according to the first large population-based study in the field, led by researchers at Karolinska Institutet and published in JAMA Neurology.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-i.title: International study helps support FDA approval of HIV drug for newborns
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-i.summary: An international study conducted through the International Maternal Pediatric Adolescent AIDS Clinical Trials (IMPAACT) Network, including researchers at the University of California San Diego, helped inform the U.S. Food and Drug Administration's (FDA) recent approval of dolutegravir, a second-generation integrase inhibitor, for the treatment of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV-1) in newborns from birth. The study, published in The Lancet HIV, identified a dosing regimen that achieves appropriate drug levels in full-term newborns, supporting the use of dolutegravir to treat HIV from the first days of life.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-r.title: Study reveals how melanoma outmaneuvers both drugs and immune defenses
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-r.summary: Melanoma is one of the most difficult cancers to treat due to its resistance to targeted drug therapies. But a new study from the University of Kentucky Markey Cancer Center shows that the cancer is playing offense as well as defense: In addition to forming resistance against the MAPK inhibitors that are commonly used to treat it, the cancer also actively suppresses the immune cells that would otherwise help eliminate it.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.title: Cardiac MRI reveals distinct mechanisms in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.summary: In heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), the heart's pumping function is largely maintained, yet the heart is unable to fill adequately with blood. A multicenter study by the German Center for Cardiovascular Research (DZHK) now shows that advanced MRI techniques can detect changes in myocardial tissue associated with different mechanisms of impaired cardiac filling. The findings from the DECIPHER HFpEF study have been published in JACC: Cardiovascular Imaging.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.title: New AI platform helps uncover promising cancer drug combinations
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.summary: UCLA investigators have developed a new artificial intelligence-based platform that could help scientists identify promising drug combinations to overcome treatment resistance in cancer.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-g.title: New gene-editing approach shows promise in treating Huntington's disease in mice
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-g.summary: Huntington's disease is caused by repetitive "stutters" in DNA—specifically repeated CAG sequences—that expand abnormally over time, leading to toxic protein accumulation that contributes to the progression of the disease. There is currently no cure for this rare and fatal genetic disease.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-d.title: No disease recurrences after short course of neoadjuvant immunotherapy, according to follow-up
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-d.summary: A short course of neoadjuvant immunotherapy continues to show long-term outcomes in patients with locally advanced mismatch repair–deficient (dMMR) colon cancer. In the NICHE-2 study, none of the 111 patients in the primary efficacy population experienced disease recurrence, and all were alive at their most recent follow-up. The findings, now published in The Lancet, provide further evidence of the durability of response to neoadjuvant immunotherapy in this patient population.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-s.title: Smart adhesive patch sticks securely and releases gently without damaging skin
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-s.summary: Most people remember the sharp sting of removing a bandage from the knee. For people with fragile skin, however, this moment can be more than brief discomfort. In neonates, older adults and critically ill patients, repeated attachment and removal of medical adhesives can cause irritation, epidermal damage and even skin stripping.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-l.title: Liver tumors form without detectable driver mutations in mice, revealing epigenetic route
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-l.summary: Cancers can develop through epigenetic pathways even without driver gene mutations (DGMs), according to a study from Science Tokyo. Researchers uncovered the YAP1–TEAD–TET1 axis, which triggers DNA demethylation and activates multiple oncogenes in hepatocellular carcinoma. Suppressing TET1 reduced tumor formation in mice, while analysis of human liver disease data supported the relevance of these findings. This study reveals an alternative epigenetic route to cancer development and offers new insights into DGM-negative cancers.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-f.title: France reports first human Shamonda virus case, says no health risk
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-f.summary: French health authorities said Thursday that the Shamonda virus, which usually affects livestock, had been detected in a human for the first time, in a severely immunocompromised patient who died earlier this month.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.title: How L-carnitine, found in red meat and exercise supplements, may amplify inflammation
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.summary: In a study published Oct. 19 in Cell, Yale researchers identified a previously unknown mechanism by which a nutrient abundant in red meat and commonly used in exercise supplements may amplify inflammation.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-b.title: Your brain maps out numbers, including integers and fractions
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-b.summary: From learning to count to solving complex calculations, math requires an inherent organization of information. A team of researchers led by Stanislas Dehaene, Ph.D., and Daniela Valério, Ph.D., at the INSERM-CEA Cognitive Neuroimaging Unit (Unicog) Lab in France took dynamic brain scans of adults presented with fractions and integers. Their findings, published on Oct. 22 in the journal PLOS Biology, revealed a map of brain activity that underlies how we arrange numerical information.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-m.title: Mental health support for parents after pediatric intensive care may modestly reduce PTSD and depressive symptoms
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-m.summary: Admission to a pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) can have lasting psychological effects on both children receiving treatment and their parents. To investigate the effects of psychosocial interventions on parents' emotional health, researchers searched five major academic databases for studies published through January 2026 and analyzed eight randomized controlled trials evaluating psychosocial interventions in parents of children admitted to the PICU. The interventions included visits to follow-up clinics, psychological screening with referral, telephone-based psychoeducation, palliative care consultations and acceptance and commitment therapy delivered via videoconference. The findings a

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.title: Comprehensive DNA sequencing reveals hidden drivers of cancer
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.summary: Michigan's Oncology Sequencing Program, or MiOncoSeq, was the first of its kind in the nation to sequence patient tumors. Launched in 2010, the program analyzes DNA and RNA from normal tissue and tumors to identify alterations that could help guide treatment.

https://theconversation.com/surviving-ca.title: Surviving cancer starts at diagnosis and continues after treatment – earlier survivorship care can help patients feel better and live longer
https://theconversation.com/surviving-ca.summary: Cancer survivorship is often thought to begin after a patient receives their last treatment. But planning for life after cancer is critical to effective care.

https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.title: One of Earth’s most powerful supervolcanoes is refilling with fresh magma
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.summary: Deep beneath Japan’s Kikai caldera, a massive magma reservoir is refilling 7,300 years after one of the most powerful volcanic eruptions in Earth's recent geological history. Scientists used underwater seismic surveys to reveal a vast store of magma that appears to have accumulated since the ancient catastrophe. The discovery could help explain how supervolcanoes like Yellowstone and Toba rebuild their magma supplies.

https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.title: Nearly 20% of Switzerland’s glacier ice has vanished in just five years
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.summary: Switzerland’s glaciers are disappearing at an alarming rate, losing more than 5% of their ice volume in 2026 alone. Some of the country’s most famous glaciers experienced their worst melting on record, while several smaller glaciers vanished completely. Nearly 20% of Switzerland’s glacier ice has disappeared in just five years, driven by unusually snowless winters and extreme summer heat.

https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.title: Dental implants can hijack your immune system, scientists discover
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.summary: Researchers have uncovered a surprising reason dental implant infections often resist antibiotics: the implants themselves can contribute to the problem. Bacteria corrode titanium implants, releasing microscopic particles that hijack immune cells, trigger destructive inflammation, and accelerate jawbone loss.

https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.title: Cambridge scientists create a $10 chip that could put a medical lab on your wrist
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.summary: Cambridge researchers have created a groundbreaking $10 optical sensor that delivers the precision of laboratory equipment in a device small enough for wearable technology. It identified foods, plastics, and medicines with 100% accuracy in tests and demonstrated the ability to monitor blood glucose, alcohol, and other health markers without invasive procedures.

https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.title: Breakthrough PTSD treatment achieves 68% remission rate in clinical trial
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.summary: A newly FDA-cleared PTSD treatment uses personalized brain mapping and magnetic stimulation to target abnormal brain activity, with a clinical trial reporting a 52% reduction in symptoms and 68% remission. Researchers believe the technology could transform PTSD care and pave the way for more precise treatments for other mental health conditions.

https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.summary: MIT engineers have built a paper-thin swimming robot powered by living muscle cells that respond to flashes of light, allowing it to swim and steer through water. The breakthrough could pave the way for tiny, self-healing biological robots capable of exploring fragile environments that ordinary machines cannot safely navigate.

https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.title: Scientists discover a surprising double benefit of exercise for Parkinson’s
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.summary: A seven-year study found that people with Parkinson’s disease who were more physically active experienced slower declines in memory, thinking, and movement abilities. Those exercising more than eight hours per week showed almost no average cognitive decline, suggesting that staying active may offer important benefits as the disease progresses.

https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.title: Scientists discover a hidden messaging system deep inside the brain
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.summary: A tiny region deep within the brain has surprised scientists by revealing a remarkably sophisticated communication system. Previously thought to broadcast the same chemical signal throughout the brain, this region actually sends targeted messages that help control learning, attention, and behavior, according to new research in mice.
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.text: Deep within the brainstem is a tiny group of nerve cells that plays an outsized role in how the brain functions. This region, called the locus coeruleus (LC), gets its name from the Latin words for "blue place." Although it contains only a small fraction of the brain's neurons, it produces norepinephrine (NE), a chemical messenger that helps regulate attention, learning, heart rate, and the body's reactions to stress and excitement. Scientists have long assumed that the LC operates like a loudspeaker, sending essentially the same norepinephrine signal across the brain. However, a new study published in Nature challenges that understanding. Using brain imaging, recordings of neural activity, genetic techniques, and behavioral experiments in mice, researchers at the Allen Institute discovered that the LC communicates through several distinct pathways. Rather than broadcasting one general message, it delivers signals to specific destinations, with different groups of neurons responding to different experiences. By tracing the connections of LC neurons, researchers found that different groups of cells communicate with specific regions of the nervous system. These pathways determine where signals trigger the release of norepinephrine, creating a much more organized communication network than previously recognized. Neurons in the upper (dorsal) portion of the LC primarily connect to the cerebral cortex and forebrain. Meanwhile, cells in the lower (ventral) portion send their signals mainly to the brainstem and spinal cord. This arrangement allows different parts of the LC to influence separate brain functions. "The findings suggest the brain's norepinephrine system is far more like a targeted postal network than a foghorn," said Karel Svoboda, director of Neural Dynamics at the Allen Institute and study co-author. Understanding how this signaling network is organized could eventually change how certain neurological and mental health conditions are treated. Norepinephrine plays a central role in regulating attention and mood, making it an important target for medications used to treat depression, anxiety, and ADHD. Neurons in the LC are also among the earliest brain cells to deteriorate in Alzheimer's disease, suggesting that the new findings could have implications for understanding and treating these conditions. Current treatments that influence norepinephrine can affect multiple brain circuits at once, sometimes producing beneficial effects in one region while causing unwanted effects elsewhere. A clearer map of the LC's specialized pathways could help scientists develop therapies that act more selectively on the circuits involved in particular symptoms. The research received support from the National Institutes of Health's Brain Research Through Advancing Innovative Neurotechnologies ® Initiative, also known as The BRAIN Initiative®. The researchers also uncovered an important distinction between the functions of different LC neurons. Cells in the dorsal LC that connect to the cortex were particularly active during learning. When mice performed decision-making tasks and adjusted their choices after an unfavorable result, these neurons increased their activity. Neurons in the ventral LC behaved differently. Their activity rose shortly before mice ignored signals indicating that a reward might be available. This suggests that these cells help regulate whether animals respond to opportunities in their surroundings. "What emerged was a clear map: neurons in the dorsal LC that send signals upward to the cortex are involved in learning, whereas neurons in the ventral region projecting downward to the brainstem and spinal cord govern whether animals engage with their environment at all," said Svoboda. "We also showed that these anatomical differences are mirrored by distinct gene expression patterns." These findings indicate that the differences between the two groups extend beyond their locations and connections. They also have distinct patterns of gene activity that reflect their specialized roles. The study involved an extensive examination of the mouse brain. Scientists used whole-brain imaging to study nearly 35,000 neurons, analyzed the genetic profiles of almost 400,000 cells, and reconstructed the complete structures of several exceptionally complex nerve cells. During this work, they encountered another remarkable finding: LC neurons possess extraordinarily long axons. These projections carry signals from nerve cells to other cells, allowing information to travel across the nervous system. The researchers found that LC axons measured approximately 35 centimeters long on average. One particularly extraordinary axon had a total reconstructed length of 70.32 centimeters, making it part of the longest single neuron ever measured in a mouse. "This neuron, like many others that we studied, supplies NE to a very large volume of the cerebral cortex. For the brain, this is highly unusual. Most neurons are more specific in their targets," said Jeremiah Cohen, scientist at the Allen Institute and study co-author. "But this neuron doesn't release NE everywhere. It ignores the cerebellum, brainstem, and spinal cord." Despite its remarkable length and extensive reach, the neuron does not distribute norepinephrine throughout the entire brain. Instead, its connections remain selective, reinforcing the discovery that the LC operates through carefully organized signaling pathways. The researchers also identified intriguing similarities between the norepinephrine system and the brain's dopamine signaling system. Dopamine is another major chemical messenger that sends signals to the basal ganglia, a brain region involved in forming habits. Scientists suspect that dopamine and norepinephrine work together to support learning, potentially allowing the brain to acquire several complex and abstract concepts at the same time. By revealing the intricate connections, specialized functions, and unusual physical structure of neurons in the locus coeruleus, the research provides a more detailed picture of how the animal brain communicates and learns. Although the findings come from experiments in mice, they could eventually help scientists better understand human brain function and design treatments that target specific neural circuits rather than affecting entire signaling systems. https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.title: A tiny defect in a crystal reveals a big quantum surprise
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.summary: Researchers have solved a long-standing challenge in understanding how tiny defects in materials like diamond and silicon carbide behave when exposed to light. Their new computational method revealed a surprisingly important energy-loss mechanism in silicon carbide that scientists had previously underestimated. The finding helps explain a mystery that has puzzled researchers for years and could improve the design of quantum computers and sensors.

https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.title: Nearly 3,000 exploding stars challenge our understanding of the Universe
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.summary: A massive analysis of 2,884 exploding stars has uncovered new evidence that dark energy, the mysterious force accelerating the universe’s expansion, may change over time. The findings challenge a cornerstone of modern cosmology and could reshape our understanding of how the universe works.

https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.title: 40 years later, Chernobyl's nuclear fallout is not what scientists expected
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.summary: Forty years after the Chornobyl disaster, tiny radioactive particles still linger in the soil, carrying a dangerous legacy. Using powerful X-rays, scientists discovered that some of these particles have remained surprisingly stable, trapping radioactive substances inside instead of releasing them into the environment.

https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.title: Scientists discover a hidden immune weapon against deadly lung cancer
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.summary: Researchers have uncovered a hidden immune defense capable of attacking small cell lung cancer, an extremely aggressive disease that often escapes conventional treatments. The specialized immune cells can recognize and destroy cancer cells even when tumors have disguised themselves from the immune system.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-artemis-cr.title: Artemis I: Crystals of experimental detectors record radiation doses near the moon
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-artemis-cr.summary: Do cosmic radiation doses near the moon differ significantly from those received by astronauts in low Earth orbit? Experimental lithium fluoride detectors, installed aboard the Orion spacecraft during the Artemis I mission, have now made it possible to obtain preliminary estimates.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-dna-cell-f.title: DNA programs a cell-free material to build its own motors and move
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-dna-cell-f.summary: Researchers have created a material that manufactures the proteins responsible for cell movement, without needing intact living cells. By embedding cell-free gene expression into a thin sheet of protein filaments, they were able to make the material wrinkle, rise into blister-like shapes and break into bundles that flow around one another.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-cell-inter.title: Mapping the cell: International research team investigates the endoplasmic reticulum
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-cell-inter.summary: Human cells contain billions of molecules. To prevent complete chaos, these molecules and the reactions between them are organized within structures known as organelles. One of the cell's most important organelles is the endoplasmic reticulum, a dynamic network that extends throughout the cell and plays an essential role in cell growth. Using a method they developed themselves, an international team of molecular biologists and bioinformaticians has tackled the challenge of determining precisely which molecules make up the membrane of this organelle. The researchers have published their findings in the journal EMBO Reports.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-metal-nasa.title: Pedal to the metal: NASA's Psyche heads toward asteroid belt
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-metal-nasa.summary: With a successful Mars gravity assist in its rearview mirror, NASA's Psyche spacecraft has fired up its thrusters and is accelerating toward the metal-rich asteroid of the same name. During the first leg of its journey, following an October 2023 launch, the mission used its electric propulsion system intermittently to maneuver into the right position to harness Mars' gravity for a propellant-saving speed boost and a slight trajectory change.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-pfas.html.title: US drinking water could contain double the reported PFAS levels, model estimates
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-pfas.html.summary: Common ways of reporting perfluoroalkyl and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS)—the man-made, so-called forever chemicals that pose environmental and health threats—could underestimate the concentration of PFAS in U.S. drinking water by as much as half, according to a study being published Oct. 23 in Cell Reports Sustainability.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-nasa-hubbl.title: NASA's Hubble charts path for Roman with gravitational lenses
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-nasa-hubbl.summary: A sweeping barred spiral galaxy marks the spot in this image, but the real treasure is the gravitational lens in the lower-right corner, where a distant background galaxy is being magnified and distorted by the gravity of a closer galaxy.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-science-al.title: When computer science meets the alpaca immune system
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-science-al.summary: After earning bachelor's and Ph.D. degrees in bioengineering with a focus on molecular biology, Will White, a postdoctoral scholar in the Department of Computer Science at Tufts, was pretty certain his future research would involve things like DNA and proteins. What he didn't know was that alpacas would also be part of the equation.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-glass-good.title: What makes glass good at conducting heat? Sound holds the key
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-glass-good.summary: Glass can keep a drink safely contained, protect a smartphone screen, or serve as a foundation for electronic components. But when it comes to controlling heat, this familiar material still holds some scientific mysteries. Now, researchers have identified a key factor governing how efficiently heat travels through silicate glass, offering a new guideline for designing glass materials for next-generation electronic devices.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-whale-ai-t.title: How to speak whale: AI uses eight to ten click sequences to predict sperm whales' feeding dives
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-whale-ai-t.summary: Arriving on the Caribbean island of Dominica for the first time "feels a little bit like stepping into Jurassic Park," said Giovanni Petri, a professor in the Network Science Institute at Northeastern University London.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-gentle-gra.title: From 'gentle' and 'graceful' to the 'cane toad of the sky': How Australia turned on the common myna
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-gentle-gra.summary: The common myna is sometimes referred to as "Australia's most hated bird." Originally from South and Central Asia, the introduced species from the starling family is abundant, raucous and bold.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-antarctic-.title: Sinking Antarctic ice reveals a hidden lake's massive water loss
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-antarctic-.summary: The Kronshtadskiy subglacial lake near East Antarctica's Amery Ice Shelf was hidden beneath Antarctica's ice, but its drainage left a mark visible from space as a broad depression that deepened by more than 6 meters (20 feet) at its center.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-voter-supp.title: What does voter suppression have to do with health?
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-voter-supp.summary: Public health researchers have long examined how societal forces can shape health outcomes. Decades after redlining was outlawed, for example, researchers continue to document its lasting effects on life expectancy, chronic disease and access to health care resources in many communities.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-el-nio-1.h.title: El Niño then and now
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-el-nio-1.h.summary: El Niño is part of a natural climate pattern that occurs roughly every two to seven years, bringing warmer-than-normal water to parts of the equatorial Pacific. The most recent very strong El Niño events, in 1997–98 and 2015–16, upended weather patterns. Impacts spanned the planet, from fires in Indonesia and the Amazon to crop failures due to drought in southern Africa to heavy rain and coastal flooding in Southern California. The current El Niño rivals these past heavyweights.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-quick-cris.title: A quick squeeze helps CRISPR turn skin cells into neurons more efficiently
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-quick-cris.summary: Human cells hold about two meters (6.6 feet) of DNA, folded and compacted to fit inside a nucleus. That packing is essential for life, but it creates a problem for scientists. Some of the genes that control a cell's identity are buried so deep in tightly packed DNA that gene-targeting tools such as CRISPR activation, or CRISPRa, struggle to reach them.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-youth-prot.title: Youth protests across Europe: The overlapping crises facing Gen Z
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-youth-prot.summary: Young people are facing a future that feels increasingly uncertain. Although every generation experiences turbulence while navigating adolescence, the pressures experienced by Gen Z—those born between 1997 and 2012—are different and seem more pervasive.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-excavation.title: Excavation reveals history of Portuguese village shelled after sheltering Spanish refugees
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-excavation.summary: Led by Dr. Rui Gomes Coelho, assistant professor of historical archaeology, the research reveals ordinary people's attitudes toward hospitality and solidarity in 20th-century Europe.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-east-asia-.title: East Asia's summer rain belt has shifted north over decades, reshaping rain and heat risks
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-east-asia-.summary: A joint research team from KAIST and the APEC Climate Center has found that the East Asian summer front has migrated north over the past half century, with the shift exceeding 200 km (124 miles) in late summer. This raises the risk that the Korean Peninsula will experience heavy rain and heat stress at the same time. The findings suggest that summer disaster planning should address flood prevention and heat-illness management together, through late September.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-agricultur.title: Time to tap into agriculture's hidden genetic potential
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-agricultur.summary: Modern agriculture's selective breeding of crops for particular requirements may now be a roadblock to further gains, prompting a trio of senior University of Queensland plant scientists to call for a new way forward.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-quantum-ca.title: Experiment shows when quantum 'cat' states stop bouncing back
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-quantum-ca.summary: Quantum systems can occupy superpositions, quantum states that combine different possibilities. For instance, a microwave field can be prepared in a superposition of an empty state and a state that contains microwave light.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-overweight.title: Study finds lower rates of overweight among vegan-fed cats
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-overweight.summary: A large-scale survey has found cats fed vegan diets had lower rates of obesity and related health problems than those fed conventional meat-based diets.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-world-expe.title: The world's most expensive spice could provide a lifeline to Colorado farmers
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-world-expe.summary: Alexander the Great, king of the ancient Greek kingdom of Macedon, reportedly bathed in saffron to heal his battle wounds. Doctors once prescribed this rare plant as a treatment for the bubonic plague. Cleopatra even used it as a fragrance to entice potential suitors. And now, this tiny flower associated with the Middle East could have a new use: providing Colorado farmers with supplemental income in the drought-stricken American West.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-window-cog.title: Hide-and-seek for treats offers a new window into cognitive decline in dogs
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-window-cog.summary: It is tough to watch a dog deal with issues associated with aging. A senior dog that gets lost at home or starts showing more anxiety may be exhibiting signs of dementia. But by the time these signs show up, the decline may have been underway for years.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-highlights.title: Study highlights gender gap in AI media coverage in Spain
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-highlights.summary: A media "glass ceiling" exists in news stories on artificial intelligence (AI) published in Spanish media in recent years: men are the main subjects in 41% of news reports, compared to just 5% featuring women. This is one of the findings of the report "InfoIA: Analysis of Information on Artificial Intelligence Published in Digital Media," conducted by the University Institute of Gender Studies at Universidad Carlos III de Madrid (UC3M).

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-ai-agents-.title: AI agents can form political camps—and changing their conversation partners does little to soften their views
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-ai-agents-.summary: Give AI agents political positions, ask them to defend their views and persuade one another, and let them decide which contacts to keep. This recent experiment, published in Nature Communications, found that over repeated exchanges, something familiar emerged: opposing camps that increasingly prefer their own company.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-red-crown-.title: What is red crown rot? Expert explains emerging soybean pathogen
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-red-crown-.summary: Red crown rot, a fungal disease of soybean, is not new to the Midwest. First reported in Illinois in 2018, the disease is now surging across the state and the region. Boris Camiletti, a plant pathologist at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, is leading the effort to understand and combat the scourge, along with the Crop Protection Network, the Illinois Soybean Association, the United Soybean Board and researchers in surrounding states.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-world-glac.title: Just 3% of the world's glaciers account for over half of glacier ice loss
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-world-glac.summary: Glaciers ending in lakes, oceans or ice shelves make up 3.2% of the world's glaciers, but lost 134 billion metric tons (148 billion tons) of ice each year between 2000 and 2019, accounting for more than half of all glacier ice loss, a new study shows.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-taiwan-typ.title: Taiwan shuts down as Typhoon Champi approaches
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-taiwan-typ.summary: Most shops and schools were shut across Taiwan on Friday as Typhoon Champi neared the island, forcing hundreds of people to leave their homes ahead of the powerful storm.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-europe-kil.title: Europe's killer heat this summer claims 50,000 lives. Climate change blamed for two-thirds of deaths
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-europe-kil.summary: Blistering record heat in Europe this summer helped kill more than 50,000 people, with nearly two-thirds of that death toll blamed on human-caused climate change, a new study found.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-based-meth.title: Light-based method enables precise control of ultrafast electron flow in a scanning tunneling microscope
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-based-meth.summary: What would it take to watch an electron move through a material? Researchers would need to see individual atoms and capture an electron's motion at incredibly short timescales. A Technion-led team has brought those two capabilities together in a scanning tunneling microscope, using carefully shaped laser pulses to control the direction of electron flow while preserving nanoscale spatial resolution.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-dead-tissu.title: Costly dead-tissue disorder in apples caused by faster growth rates
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-dead-tissu.summary: New research reveals that faster growth rates in Honeycrisp apples increase both the incidence and severity of the "bitter pit" disorder, which is responsible for large-scale fruit yield losses and avoidable economic impacts for apple producers and storers.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-p.title: What can people who remember everything teach us about the brain?
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-p.summary: Without looking back at an appointment calendar or diary or searching Google, what can you recall about the day of Nov. 5, 2021? Unless that date happens to hold an anniversary or other special meaning, probably not too much.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-d.title: Diagnostic uncertainty: Why losing a diagnosis can be as difficult as receiving one
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-d.summary: When actor Christina Applegate revealed that she had been misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosis (MS), she described the experience as "very unnerving" and "really confusing."

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-p.title: Study finds patients experienced rapid weight gain after starting antipsychotic medication
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-p.summary: People with severe mental illness experienced more rapid increases in both weight and long-term blood sugar levels during the first three months after starting treatment with antipsychotic medication, according to a study from Karolinska Institutet and University College London published in The Lancet Psychiatry.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.title: AI gets more diagnoses right than generalist doctors in medical challenge
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.summary: One of the many challenging parts of being a doctor is diagnosing exactly what is wrong with a patient. This is because numerous illnesses often have overlapping symptoms, which can make the diagnostic journey a long one.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.title: Using AI in the global fight against HIV
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.summary: When faced with the possibility of an HIV diagnosis, sometimes the best initial prescription is support from a trusted friend—someone who might offer not just emotional guidance but also critical, practical health resources. A Harvard research team thinks artificial intelligence has a role to play in that process.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.title: Children who eat more ultraprocessed foods show stronger brain responses to appetizing foods
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.summary: Children who eat more ultraprocessed foods (UPFs) show stronger responses in the brain's reward network when viewing images of appetizing foods—and these brain responses are linked to increases in body fat one year later.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.title: AI breast cancer survival model could improve accuracy and personalize care
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.summary: New University of Cincinnati Cancer Center research published in the Journal of Statistical Theory and Practice describes the potential for a more robust and accurate breast cancer survival model that combines statistical methods with a deep learning framework. The goal is to give physicians a better tool to make personalized care decisions for each patient.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-t.title: Tackling diabetes with an electronic implant: How a tiny catalyst lowers blood sugar
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-t.summary: Type 2 diabetes is becoming increasingly common worldwide. Unlike type 1 diabetes, it is often linked to obesity, a sedentary lifestyle and excess energy intake over many years. Although insulin injections can bring blood sugar levels down, they do not address the body's chronic energy surplus. Insulin merely helps muscle cells take up glucose from the bloodstream, but if the body does not use that energy, the excess is converted into fat. This helps explain why many patients continue to gain weight despite treatment.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.title: AI tool may support dermatologists in assessing skin lesions for cancer risk
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.summary: Mayo Clinic researchers have found that an artificial intelligence (AI) tool may provide dermatologists with additional information to help assess whether skin lesions are cancerous and inform their clinical decisions about whether to biopsy or monitor them, according to a study published in Mayo Clinic Proceedings.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-t.title: The tendency to imitate others is shared across 22 countries, study finds
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-t.summary: People often imitate some of the actions and gestures of others they are observing, without deliberately trying to do so. This tendency, known as automatic imitation, has long been assumed to be universal.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-m.title: Who decides when medical AI may be updated?
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-m.summary: Medical AI can improve with new patient data, but every update must be checked first. Patients, equipment and ways of working change, and a model trained on older data can gradually get worse without anyone noticing.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-g.title: Gut microbiome may help explain why sleep improvement varies after hydrogen supplementation
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-g.summary: A Hiroshima University–led clinical trial found that hydrogen supplementation did not significantly improve sleep quality compared with a placebo; however, exploratory analyses suggest that differences in the abundance of hydrogen-producing gut bacteria may be associated with individual differences in sleep-related responses.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.title: How much autonomy do women actually have when giving birth?
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.summary: You spend your pregnancy researching and planning for when your baby finally arrives, as well as considering what might happen if things don't go according to plan.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-w.title: 4 ways to help your body adjust to the fall time change
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-w.summary: An extra hour in bed sounds like a good deal. But while our phones may update to the fall time change automatically, our body clock isn't quite so quick. You may even find yourself waking up earlier than normal and ready for bed before your evening has properly begun.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-w.title: Women are more optimistic about aging—until memory problems emerge
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-w.summary: A study, published in the Journal of Women & Aging, found memory complaints were linked to negative expectations about aging in people with mild cognitive impairment as well as cognitively healthy adults.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-f.title: Plant-first food pyramid brings international dietary guidelines together in adaptable global guide
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-f.summary: Dietary guidance varies by country, and no international food pyramid has brought its recommendations together until now. BYU nutritional science professor Karen Della Corte led a global team of nutrition scientists to develop an International Food Guide Pyramid that reflects broad scientific agreement and can be adapted across cultures and borders.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.title: Updated cancer treatment framework offers new guidance on actionability and resistance biomarkers
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.summary: ESMO has published version 2 of the ESMO Scale for Clinical Actionability of molecular Targets (ESCAT), a major update to the internationally recognized precision oncology framework that helps oncologists assess the clinical relevance of molecular alterations and match patients with the most appropriate targeted therapies.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-r.title: Can Reddit help strengthen health communications on extreme heat?
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-r.summary: Two years ago, Robbie M. Parks, an environmental health scientist at Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health, and Nathaniel Matthews-Trigg, director of climate and disaster resilience at Americares, founded an online community on Reddit, r/heat_prep, where members share information and advice about coping with extreme temperatures.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-m.title: Mindfulness and self-compassion can alleviate premenstrual symptoms
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-m.summary: A kind attitude toward oneself and practicing mindfulness can improve functioning in individuals who experience severe premenstrual symptoms, according to a study by psychologists from SWPS University and Jagiellonian University.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-b.title: Blood test can help clinicians better identify brain injury severity in patients
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-b.summary: Clinician-scientists hope to expand the use of blood-based biomarker tests for traumatic brain injury (TBI) to improve identification and escalation of care for patients whose diagnosis otherwise might be missed.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-k.title: First-of-its-kind trial tests low-dose radiation to target brain inflammation in Parkinson's disease
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-k.summary: Mayo Clinic researchers are studying whether low-dose radiation therapy can slow the progression of Parkinson's disease by targeting inflammation in areas of the brain affected by the disease. The clinical trial is the first to investigate low-dose radiation as an anti-inflammatory approach in patients with early-stage Parkinson's disease.

https://theconversation.com/why-ultra-or.title: Why ultra-Orthodox parties hold so much sway in Israeli politics
https://theconversation.com/why-ultra-or.summary: Ultra-Orthodox Jews, often called Haredim, make up a small but growing percentage of Israel’s population. Still, their political parties wield significant influence.

https://theconversation.com/fear-based-c.title: Fear-based campaign ads can grab attention, but whether they win votes is less clear
https://theconversation.com/fear-based-c.summary: Political campaigns often use fear to play on voters’ existing prejudices and stereotypes. What that means for your vote is less predictable.
